stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
After the city of Harlow Falls raised its minimum wage by 18 percent, economist Dalia Osei tracked staffing at 240 local restaurants. Eighteen months later, payroll head counts were essentially unchanged. Osei concluded that the higher wage floor had not reduced restaurants' use of low-wage labor.

Text 2
Osei's head counts are careful, and the restaurants did keep about as many people on staff. But a payroll lists a worker scheduled for twelve hours a week the same way it lists one scheduled for thirty, and the restaurants' time sheets show average weekly hours per employee falling by roughly a tenth.
choices: The wage increase did little to change how much low-wage labor the restaurants used.
The restaurants employed about as many workers after the increase as they had before it.
Payroll head counts cannot reveal how the restaurants adjusted to the higher wage.
Raising a city's minimum wage does not, in general, cause employers to cut jobs.
explanation: Text 1 sets up a finding (head counts stayed the same) and then draws a conclusion from it (the restaurants used no less labor). Text 2 opens by granting the finding ('the restaurants did keep about as many people on staff'). It then disputes only the conclusion, because hours per worker fell. So Text 2 qualifies Text 1. It accepts the observation and rejects the inference. The only thing both authors would accept is the observation itself: the restaurants employed about as many workers as before.

A.why: This is Text 1's final conclusion, and it is exactly what Text 2 was written to challenge. Fewer hours per worker means the restaurants used less labor even with the same head count. You saw that Text 2 concedes something, but you picked the claim it rejects instead of the one it concedes.

C.why: This gets Text 2's position right but not Text 1's. Osei relied on head counts as her evidence, so she would not accept that they miss how the restaurants adjusted. A statement that only one author holds cannot be something both would agree with.

D.why: This is a stronger version of Text 1's claim than Text 1 actually makes. Osei drew a conclusion about one city's restaurants, not about minimum wage increases in general. Text 2 also gives no support for a general rule. Neither author would sign on to a law about all employers.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
In the eleven days before a magnitude 5.4 earthquake struck the Vessel Ridge fault, seismometers recorded over 300 small tremors clustered near the eventual rupture. Geophysicist Tomas Reyna concludes that the tremors marked slow, silent slip that loaded the fault until it failed, and thus that swarms there may warn of larger shocks.

Text 2
The timing and placement of the Vessel Ridge tremors are hard to dismiss as chance. Yet fluid rising through fractured rock can raise pressure enough to set off a swarm and, days later, a larger rupture, and it is difficult to exclude that sequence. If fluid was responsible, a swarm need not reflect slow slip.
choices: The tremors reveal that slow slip was loading the fault before it ruptured.
Swarms on the Vessel Ridge fault reliably signal that a larger quake will follow.
The tremors were most likely connected to whatever produced the mainshock.
Rising fluid is the likelier source of the tremors recorded before the mainshock.
explanation: Text 1 gives an observation (a swarm of tremors just before and near the mainshock) and an explanation for it (slow slip loaded the fault). Text 2 offers a different explanation for the same observation: rising fluid could have caused both the swarm and the rupture. Text 2 does not deny the link between the swarm and the mainshock. It says the link is 'hard to dismiss as chance'. Reyna's account also ties the two together, through slow slip. The authors disagree about what the connecting cause was, but both treat the tremors as connected to the cause of the mainshock.

A.why: This is Reyna's explanation, and it is the very claim Text 2 targets. Text 2 says that if fluid was responsible, the swarm 'need not reflect slow slip.' You found the claim under attack but treated it as common ground.

B.why: This turns Text 1's claim into a stronger one than it makes. Reyna says swarms 'may warn' of larger shocks, not that they reliably do. Text 2's account suggests a swarm might show only that fluid is moving. Neither author makes a claim this strong.

D.why: This gets one text's role right and the other's wrong. Text 2 only says the fluid sequence is 'difficult to exclude'. It never says fluid is the likelier cause, and Reyna would reject the idea outright. Agreeing with a hedged alternative is different from both authors endorsing it.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Indigo-dyed cotton in the Varenna valley has long been credited to merchants who settled there in the 1680s. But textile historian Ilse Marchetti found indigo in cloth fragments radiocarbon-dated to the 1620s, and she concluded that valley weavers were dyeing with indigo decades before the merchants arrived.

Text 2
Marchetti's dates are secure, and the early fragments do carry indigo. Yet a residue shows where cloth was used, not where it was dyed. Valley households in the 1620s bought finished cloth from coastal ports, and no dye vats from that period have been found in Varenna.
choices: Weavers in the Varenna valley were dyeing cotton with indigo before the 1680s.
Indigo-dyed cloth was present in the Varenna valley before the merchants settled there.
Radiocarbon dating cannot establish when the Varenna cloth fragments were made.
The merchants who arrived in the 1680s had no part in spreading indigo dyeing.
explanation: Text 2 accepts Marchetti's dates and the indigo, then disputes only where the dyeing happened. What both texts accept, then, is that indigo cloth was already in the valley before the 1680s. Text 1 also says the cloth was dyed locally, and Text 2 rejects that part.

A.why: You picked Text 1's conclusion and assumed Text 2 shares it because Text 2 opens by agreeing. Text 2's turn ('Yet...') is aimed at exactly this claim: the cloth could have been dyed on the coast and bought ready-made.

C.why: You assumed Text 2 attacks the dating. It says the opposite ('Marchetti's dates are secure'), and Text 1 depends on those dates.

D.why: You went further than either text. Text 1 says only that the merchants did not introduce indigo first, and Text 2 says nothing about their later role.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Over three decades, thunderstorms formed 30 percent more often east of Harlow, downwind of the city, than west of it. Meteorologist Dana Okafor attributes the gap to the city's heat: pavement and roofs warm the air above them, and the rising plume, carried east by prevailing winds, seeds storms.

Text 2
Okafor's comparison is careful, and regional weather alone cannot explain the gap. But a city is also an obstacle. Dense blocks of tall buildings force incoming air upward and split approaching storm cells, which could produce the same eastern excess without any added warmth.
choices: Heat rising from Harlow's pavement and roofs is what seeds the additional storms east of it.
Some feature of Harlow itself, not regional weather, accounts for the additional storms east of it.
Tall buildings split storms that would otherwise have passed directly over Harlow's center.
Thirty years of records are too few to show a reliable difference in storm frequency.
explanation: Text 2 offers a different explanation for the same result. Okafor blames the city's heat, and Text 2 blames the city's shape. Both blame the city, though, and Text 2 says outright that regional weather cannot explain the gap. The statement both accept is that something about Harlow itself causes the extra storms.

A.why: You saw that Text 2 agrees with Okafor's comparison and assumed it also agrees with her cause. Text 2 offers buildings as a cause that works 'without any added warmth', so it does not accept heat as the cause.

C.why: This is Text 2's mechanism only. Text 1 never mentions buildings or split storm cells, so you can't say its author would agree.

D.why: Neither author questions the record. Text 1 builds on it, and Text 2 calls the comparison careful.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
In a study of 1,400 recreational runners, those assigned to stretch statically before each run reported injuries at the same rate over twelve weeks as those who did not. The researchers concluded that pre-run static stretching does nothing to protect runners from injury.

Text 2
For joggers, who make up most such samples, that conclusion is probably right: their typical injuries come from repeated impact, which stretching does not address. Sprinters are another matter. Their most common injury, the hamstring strain, occurs when a muscle is rapidly lengthened, and in trials with competitive sprinters, stretching has reduced such strains.
choices: Static stretching before a run does not lower the injury rate of runners in general.
Pre-run static stretching is unlikely to reduce injuries among recreational joggers.
Static stretching before a run reduces hamstring strains in competitive sprinters.
Joggers and sprinters tend to suffer their injuries through the same mechanism.
explanation: Text 2 narrows the claim without rejecting it. It accepts the finding for joggers ('probably right') and makes an exception for sprinters. Both authors therefore agree that stretching before a run does little for recreational joggers.

A.why: You read Text 2's opening agreement as accepting Text 1's whole conclusion. Text 1 says 'runners', and Text 2 rejects it for sprinters, who are runners too. Text 2 accepts only the narrower version of the claim.

C.why: Only Text 2 makes this claim. Text 1's own conclusion says stretching protects runners from nothing, so its author would not agree.

D.why: Text 2's argument depends on the two groups being injured differently: joggers through repeated impact, sprinters through rapid lengthening of a muscle.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Every 212 days, the star KX-17 dims by about 4 percent for nine days. Because the dimming repeats so regularly, a team led by astronomer Rafael Ostby concluded that a giant planet encircled by a broad ring system is crossing in front of the star.

Text 2
The regularity does rule out spots or flares on the star itself, which come and go on no fixed schedule. But a ringed planet at that orbital distance would cross the star in under two days. A diffuse band of dust strung out along a single orbit could block light for nine.
choices: The dimming of KX-17 results from orbiting material passing in front of the star.
A giant planet with broad rings is responsible for the regular dimming of KX-17.
The dimming of KX-17 is most likely caused by activity on the star's own surface.
Bands of dust orbiting stars commonly gather to form the rings of giant planets.
explanation: Text 2 grants Ostby's main inference, that the regular schedule means something is orbiting the star and not changing on its surface. It disputes only what that object is. A ringed planet and a band of dust are both orbiting material, so both authors accept this choice.

B.why: You took Text 1's specific conclusion as shared ground. Text 2 rejects the ringed planet because its crossing would last under two days, not nine.

C.why: Both authors reject this. Text 1 relies on the regular timing, and Text 2 says that timing rules out spots and flares on the star.

D.why: You combined the two texts' objects into a general claim about how rings form. Neither text discusses where rings come from.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Folklorist Mara Lindqvist collected forty versions of the tale of the drowned bell from villages along the Selm River. Versions told near the river's source are brief, while those told near its mouth add names, places, and a second bell. She concludes that the tale began upstream and gathered detail as it traveled downriver.

Text 2
The pattern Lindqvist documents is real, but the towns near the Selm's mouth were also the largest, and they supported paid storytellers who lengthened every tale they performed. Elaboration there may reflect who told the story, not how far it had traveled.
choices: A folktale's content can change as it is retold by different communities of tellers.
The tale of the drowned bell originated in villages near the Selm River's source.
Paid storytellers in the river-mouth towns first invented the tale of the drowned bell.
The most elaborate versions of the tale were collected near the Selm River's source.
explanation: Both texts explain the same pattern of variation differently. Lindqvist says the tale gained detail as it traveled, and Text 2 says storytellers lengthened it in performance. Either way, the tale changes when it is retold, and that is the point both authors share.

B.why: This is the claim Text 1 ends on, and Text 2 is written to challenge it. If the detail reflects who told the story, the detail is no longer evidence that the tale started upstream.

C.why: You made Text 2's point stronger than it is. Text 2 says the storytellers lengthened tales, not that they created this one, and Text 1 would reject the idea.

D.why: This reverses the pattern both texts accept. The fuller versions come from near the mouth, not the source.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Teodor Vasko's admirers described him writing whole quartets in an afternoon. His manuscripts tell a different story: nearly every page is crowded with cancellations and inserted passages. Musicologist Aiko Brandt concludes that Vasko composed slowly, reworking each piece at length before it could be performed.

Text 2
Brandt is right that the revisions are extensive. But the inks used for them did not exist until the 1840s, years after the pieces premiered, when Vasko was preparing them for print. The drafts beneath the corrections are fluent and may well have been written quickly.
choices: Vasko made extensive changes to his manuscripts after first writing out his works.
Vasko reworked each of his pieces at length before it was first performed.
Vasko's admirers were accurate in claiming he wrote whole quartets in an afternoon.
Vasko's printed scores are nearly identical to the drafts beneath his corrections.
explanation: Text 2 accepts that the revisions are extensive and disputes only when they were made. Both authors therefore agree that Vasko heavily revised his works after the first draft. They disagree about whether that happened before the premieres or decades later.

B.why: You saw that both texts agree about the revisions and carried that agreement over to their timing. The ink dates in Text 2 place the revisions after the premieres, which goes directly against this claim.

C.why: Text 2 says only that the drafts 'may well' have been written quickly, which is not the same as confirming the legend. Text 1 explicitly rejects the legend.

D.why: Text 2 says the corrections were made to prepare the pieces for print, so the printed scores would differ from the drafts.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
After a wetland was restored upstream of Corbin in 2009, hydrologists compared fifteen storms from before and after the restoration. For storms of similar size, peak river flow at Corbin fell by an average of 20 percent. The team concluded that the wetland is an effective defense against flooding in the town.

Text 2
For storms like those fifteen, the wetland clearly helps. But none approached the size of Corbin's most destructive floods. In those, days of rain saturate the wetland before the peak arrives, leaving it little capacity to absorb more water.
choices: The restored wetland lowered peak river flow at Corbin during storms like those studied.
The restored wetland is an effective defense against all of the flooding Corbin experiences.
The fifteen storms studied included several of the largest floods in Corbin's history.
Wetlands upstream of a town become saturated during most heavy rainstorms.
explanation: Text 2 limits Text 1's claim to a smaller range of storms. It accepts the result for storms like the fifteen studied ('clearly helps') and denies it only for the largest floods. Both authors agree that the wetland reduced peak flow in storms of the kind that were measured.

B.why: You stretched Text 1's conclusion until it covered every flood. Text 2 says the wetland does little in the most destructive floods, so its author would reject this.

C.why: Text 2 says none of the fifteen storms approached the size of Corbin's worst floods.

D.why: Text 2 describes saturation only during the largest, multi-day storms. It does not say this happens in most heavy storms, and Text 1 never mentions saturation.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
During a 2021 marine heat wave, corals in Tavu Lagoon, where water temperatures swing by up to 6°C each day, bleached far less than corals on the nearby outer reef. Marine biologist Sione Fifita concluded that daily exposure to fluctuating temperatures had conditioned the lagoon corals to tolerate heat.

Text 2
It is difficult to exclude another route to the same result. Over many generations, the lagoon's temperature swings may have killed off heat-sensitive corals, leaving populations descended from tolerant survivors. On that view, an outer-reef coral moved into the lagoon would gain little.
choices: The lagoon's fluctuating temperatures help account for its corals' greater heat tolerance.
Individual corals grow more heat tolerant through daily exposure to temperature swings.
Outer-reef corals moved into Tavu Lagoon would gain little resistance to heat.
Lagoon corals and outer-reef corals bleached at similar rates during the heat wave.
explanation: Text 2 offers a different explanation for the same result, but both explanations depend on the temperature swings. In Text 1, the swings condition each coral. In Text 2, they remove sensitive corals over generations. Either way, the swings help explain the lagoon corals' tolerance.

B.why: This is Text 1's mechanism. Text 2 argues that a single coral moved into the lagoon would gain little, which goes directly against this claim.

C.why: This is the prediction from Text 2's view. Text 1's conditioning explanation suggests a moved coral would gain tolerance, so its author would not agree.

D.why: Text 1 reports that lagoon corals bleached far less, and Text 2 accepts that result ('the same result').
